subject: Social Science (Exploring Society: India and Beyond)

details: Elements of nature become resources when human technology, knowledge, and skills allow their extraction and beneficial use.
Three indispensable criteria: technological accessibility, economic feasibility, and cultural/social acceptability.
evidence_or_examples: Solar radiation and wind existed for millennia but became active modern energy resources through solar panels and wind turbines.

details: Classified by origin into biotic (living/organic origins) and abiotic (non-living physical matter).
Classified by exhaustibility into renewable (replenished by natural cycles) and non-renewable (geologically finite).
evidence_or_examples: Biotic: forests, crops, livestock; Abiotic: land, minerals, water.
Renewable: solar energy, wind power, groundwater; Non-renewable: coal, crude oil, metallic ores.

branches.theme: 1.2 Categorisation and Stewardship of Natural Resources

details: Resource stewardship demands responsible use and preservation to prevent ecological degradation.
Overexploitation leads to biodiversity loss, habitat destruction, and severe depletion of non-renewable fuels.
evidence_or_examples: Excessive tube-well pumping causing coastal groundwater salinity and aquifer destruction.
Community rainwater harvesting and Thar Desert solar park projects.

details: Ecosystem functions are intrinsic ecological processes operating within biomes.
Ecosystem services are direct or indirect economic and survival benefits that human societies derive from ecosystem functions.
evidence_or_examples: Function: Soil formation and nutrient cycling; Service: Crop agriculture, clean drinking water, climate regulation.

branches.theme: 2.1 Emergence of Regional Kingdoms and the Delhi Sultanate

details: Transition from Delhi Sultanate expansion to strong independent regional states across North and South India.
Southern empires (Vijayanagara, Bahmani) maintained territorial sovereignty, commercial prosperity, and architectural patronages.
evidence_or_examples: Vijayanagara under Krishnadevaraya fostering maritime trade through West Coast ports.
Ahom Kingdom in Assam utilizing Paik land-military system and riverine defenses to repel invasions.

sub_branches.concept: Trade Guilds and Financial Credit Systems
details: Commercial expansion supported by merchant associations (shrenis) and traditional banking houses (sarafs).
Hundis allowed long-distance capital transfers and credit settlements without physical movement of gold/silver.
evidence_or_examples: Bustling trade networks in medieval port cities like Surat, Calicut, and Hooghly.
Merchants traveling from Agra to Golconda utilizing Hundis for risk-free transactions.

details: Centralized bureaucratic integration via the Mansabdari system assigning military/administrative ranks (Zat and Sawar).
Scientific land measurement and standardized revenue assessment introduced by Raja Todar Mal (Zabt system).
evidence_or_examples: 10-year survey (1570-1580) tracking crop yields, market prices, and cultivated area in bighas.
Classification of land fertility into Polaj, Parauti, Chachar, and Banjar.

branches.theme: 3.1 Foundations of Swarajya and Strategic Forts

sub_branches.concept: Ideology of Hindavi Swarajya and Cultural Roots
details: Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj united local deshmukhs under the vision of sovereign self-rule (Swarajya).
Cultural foundation built by Bhakti saints preaching social equality and unity in vernacular Marathi.
evidence_or_examples: Teachings of Sant Tukaram, Sant Dnyaneshwar, and Samarth Ramdas creating broad social cohesion.

sub_branches.concept: Terrain-Integrated Fort Architecture and Naval Force
details: Fortresses served as administrative capitals, military depots, and defensive sanctuaries.
Shivaji constructed coastal sea forts and established a permanent naval fleet to counter maritime powers.
evidence_or_examples: Hill fort Pratapgad and sea fort Sindhudurg with double curtain walls and hidden entryways (Maha Darwaja).
Naval commanders like Kanhoji Angre securing West Coast waters.

sub_branches.concept: Ganimi Kava and Tax Collection Models
details: Military strategy relied on light cavalry, rapid mobility, surprise attacks, and intimate terrain knowledge (Ganimi Kava).
Revenue generated from external territories through Chauth (25% tax) and Sardeshmukhi (10% additional head tax).
evidence_or_examples: Ambushes in Western Ghats mountain passes against larger imperial armies.
Levying protection taxes on border Mughal and Deccan provinces.

sub_branches.concept: Governance under Ashta Pradhan and Women Rulers
details: Central administrative council of eight ministers (Ashta Pradhan) with state records maintained in Modi script.
Maratha leadership sustained by visionary women rulers and expansion under Peshwas.
evidence_or_examples: Maharani Tarabai leading Maratha war of independence against Aurangzeb.
Rani Ahilyabai Holkar of Malwa rebuilding temples, roads, and promoting fair governance.

details: European trading companies (Portuguese, Dutch, French, British) established fortified trade posts (factories).
East India Company transformed from trader to territorial sovereign through victories at Plassey (1757) and Buxar (1764).
evidence_or_examples: Portuguese Cartaz naval pass system.
Diplomatic annexation tools: Subsidiary Alliance (Lord Wellesley) and Doctrine of Lapse (Lord Dalhousie).

branches.theme: 4.2 Impact of British Policies: Economic Exploitation and Resistance
branches.full_notes: Colonial land revenue policies and industrial market destruction triggered widespread resistance.

details: Unfair tariff barriers placed on Indian handloom exports while British machine-manufactured goods flooded local markets.
Systematic transfer of Indian financial surplus and resources to Britain without economic return.
evidence_or_examples: Ruin of weaver communities in Bengal and Varanasi.
Dadabhai Naoroji's Drain of Wealth economic analysis.

sub_branches.concept: Land Revenue Systems and Uprisings Leading to 1857
details: Rigid land tax extraction models (Permanent Settlement, Ryotwari, Mahalwari) forced widespread peasant debt and land alienation.
Widespread discontent exploded in tribal revolts (Santhal, Munda) and culminated in the Great Rebellion of 1857.
evidence_or_examples: Santhal Rebellion (1855) against moneylenders (dikus) and British police.
Government of India Act 1858 transferring power from Company to British Crown.

chapters.chapter_title: Universal Franchise and India’s Electoral System

mind_map.root_topic: Universal Franchise and India’s Electoral System

branches.theme: 5.1 Constitutional Foundation of Universal Adult Franchise

details: Article 326 guarantees voting rights to every citizen aged 18 and above without discrimination.
Rejected colonial property/literacy restrictions to establish absolute political equality and dignity.
evidence_or_examples: Adopted in 1950, granting equal voting power to 173 million citizens in the 1st general election (1951-52).

sub_branches.concept: Election Commission of India (ECI) and Voting System
details: Autonomous constitutional body managing elections, electoral rolls, and enforcing the Model Code of Conduct.
Uses First-Past-The-Post (FPTP) system where candidate with plurality of valid votes wins constituency seat.
evidence_or_examples: Administrative pyramid from Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) to Returning Officers (RO) and Polling Booth Officers.
Deployment of Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs) and Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail (VVPAT).

details: Constitutional reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes (SC) and Scheduled Tribes (ST) to ensure fair legislative voice.
Accessible voting provisions for elderly voters (85+), Persons with Disabilities (PwD), and remote populations.
evidence_or_examples: Home voting via postal ballots for elderly/PwD voters and Braille signage on EVMs.
Setting up single-voter polling stations in Gir Forest and high Himalayan mountain terrains.

chapters.chapter_title: The Parliamentary System: Legislature and Executive

mind_map.root_topic: The Parliamentary System: Legislature and Executive

branches.theme: 6.1 Bicameral Legislature: Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha

details: Parliament comprises the President of India and two houses: Lok Sabha (House of the People) and Rajya Sabha (Council of States).
Lok Sabha directly represents citizens (543 seats, 5-year term); Rajya Sabha represents states indirectly (245 seats, permanent body).
evidence_or_examples: Lok Sabha dissolved every 5 years or sooner; 1/3rd of Rajya Sabha members retire every 2 years.

details: Propose Bill → First Reading → Second Reading (clause-by-clause scrutiny) → Third Reading → Passing in House 1 → House 2 → Presidential Assent → Act.
Money Bills deal strictly with taxation and expenditure; can only be introduced in Lok Sabha.
evidence_or_examples: Rajya Sabha has 14 days to review Money Bills before they are automatically deemed passed.

details: Executive (Prime Minister & Council of Ministers) remains directly answerable to the elected Lok Sabha.
Oversight tools include Question Hour, Zero Hour, Parliamentary Standing Committees, and No-Confidence Motions.
evidence_or_examples: Question Hour allowing MPs to ask starred questions demanding oral answers from ministers.
Departmentally Related Standing Committees scrutinizing ministry demands for grants.

branches.theme: 7.1 Core Inputs of Production: Land, Labour, and Capital

details: Land encompasses all free gifts of nature (soil, water, forests, minerals, air).
Labour represents physical or mental human effort exerted to produce goods and services for income.
evidence_or_examples: Farmland, water reservoirs, and mineral reserves acting as Land inputs.
Skilled factory operators, software developers, and farm workers acting as Labour inputs.

sub_branches.concept: Physical Capital: Fixed versus Working Capital
details: Physical capital represents man-made inputs required for manufacturing.
Fixed Capital includes durable assets used over multiple years; Working Capital consists of single-use operational inputs.
evidence_or_examples: Fixed: Heavy machinery, factory buildings, tube-wells, tractors.
Working: Raw cotton, timber, fuel, cash for wage payments.

details: Entrepreneurship organizes land, labour, and capital, implements innovations, and bears business risk.
Human Capital is built through education, vocational training, healthcare, and productive workplace culture.
evidence_or_examples: J.R.D. Tata and modern young innovators driving industrial enterprises.
Skill development through SWAYAM portal and adoption of Japanese Kaizen continuous improvement philosophy.
